props.title: Not Easily Broken

sections.content: Not Easily Broken (2009) represents a pivotal entry in African-American faith-based cinema, directed by Bill Duke and based on T.D. Jakes' novel. The film follows a similar thematic path as Fireproof (2008) and War Room (2015), examining marriage through a Christian lens while tackling real-world challenges. Like Why Did I Get Married? (2007), it presents an authentic portrayal of middle-class Black couples navigating relationship struggles, career pressures, and faith.

sections.content: The film's exploration of marriage under pressure connects strongly to other relationship dramas like Just Wright (2010) and Something New (2006). Director Bill Duke brings the same careful attention to character development seen in his earlier work Cover (2007), allowing Morris Chestnut and Taraji P. Henson to create a believable couple whose faith is tested by tragedy and temptation.

What sets Not Easily Broken apart is its unflinching look at masculinity within African-American marriages, similar to themes explored in The Family That Preys (2008) and This Christmas (2007). The film addresses how career setbacks, family interference, and personal trauma can strain even the strongest relationships while maintaining hope through faith. sections.content: The film arrived during a surge of African-American faith-based films like The Gospel (2005) and Kings Faith (2013). Unlike mainstream romantic dramas, these films specifically address how spirituality shapes relationship dynamics in the Black community. The success of Not Easily Broken helped pave the way for more nuanced explorations of faith and marriage in films like Black or White (2014) and The Good Fight (2012).
